title: Nodics as Data as a Service
readerIntent: Evaluate Nodics as a governed business-data platform.
priorKnowledge: Understand APIs, schemas, security, search, import/export, and operations.
owner: Composed Nodics data, API, security, search, import/export, and operational capabilities
summary: Nodics can expose tenant-safe business data through stable APIs, search, imports, exports, events, workflows, and BackOffice while each domain retains ownership.

sections.heading: What is Nodics as Data as a Service?
paragraphs: Data as a Service (DaaS) makes governed business data available through stable APIs and contracts rather than application-specific database access. Consumers request approved views of data while the owning capability preserves validation, security, tenancy, and lifecycle rules.
Think of an internal data counter: authorized consumers ask for a defined product instead of entering the records archive and constructing their own unofficial copy.

sections.heading: Business outcomes
items: Centralize governed data definitions without coupling consumers to database providers.
Deliver API and search access to websites, mobile clients, partners, operations, and assistants.
Accelerate new customer applications through reusable schemas, services, routes, permissions, and observability.
Support PIM, content, commerce, logistics, and partner-defined domains through modules.

sections.heading: Adoption path
items: Identify authoritative domains, owners, consumers, tenant/enterprise scopes, service objectives, and regulatory constraints.
Reuse or extend existing schemas before creating new models.
Expose least-privilege versioned APIs and query contracts.
Configure providers, import/export, cache/search, events/workflows, audit, backup, and recovery.
Validate isolation, performance, failure, migration, and operational evidence before production.

sections.heading: Example: centralized product information
items: A business centralizes product identity and attributes in Product, contextual prices in Pricing, stock in Inventory, units in Units, and presentation content in CMS. Each capability retains authority while consumers receive composed contracts.
Business users author staged data and use workflows for manual and automatic validation and approval. nPublish sends exact approved versions to an Online target designed for customer traffic.
Websites, mobile clients, marketplaces, and partners call versioned APIs or approved search projections. Cache and search accelerate reads but can be rebuilt from authoritative data.
This delivers PIM-like and DaaS outcomes without placing every domain in one generic table or exposing database collections directly.

sections.heading: Consumer and provider contracts
items: Consumers authenticate with the appropriate human or service identity, receive least-privilege projections, preserve tenant context, use pagination and idempotency, and handle documented errors and rate limits.

Owning modules define schemas, validation, authorization, lifecycle, APIs, events, imports, exports, and service objectives. Provider adapters implement database, cache, search, or event technology behind those contracts.
Adding a third-party provider follows registration, configuration, capability declaration, qualification, observability, failure mapping, and fallback rules; business modules do not import its SDK.
Contract evolution uses compatible versions, migration, deprecation evidence, consumer testing, and rollback rather than changing stored data and hoping every client adapts.

sections.heading: Limits
paragraphs: DaaS is a composition of implemented capabilities, not an unrestricted database endpoint. Consumers cannot bypass target authorization, validation, ownership, or provider-neutral service contracts.

sections.heading: Production acceptance
items: Verify tenant and enterprise isolation, ownership, field masking, API exposure, service audiences, cross-module relationships, import/export authorization, and safe diagnostics.
Measure latency, throughput, pagination, indexing lag, cache behavior, provider saturation, publication lag, availability, backup/restore, and recovery against explicit service objectives.

Test provider outage, partial derived refresh, duplicate import, schema migration, consumer retry, stale contract, event duplication, search rebuild, cache loss, and regional or regulatory constraints.
Provide business ownership, data dictionary, beginner consumer guide, developer extension guide, OpenAPI or contract reference, operational runbooks, incident responsibility, and known limitations.

sections.heading: Complete guide: How To Use Nodics As Data As A Service
paragraphs: Data as a Service, or DaaS, is a Nodics platform pattern. It is not a separate module that must exist by that name.

In Nodics, DaaS means using the platform as a governed data lake, data hub, or product information center. Data can enter from many sources, move through validation and transformation, become searchable and versioned where required, and then leave through export contracts that match each target system.

sections.heading: Beginner Summary
paragraphs: DaaS means Nodics can become the trusted center for data movement and data quality.
For a beginner, think about four stages:

| Stage | Nodics responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Intake | Receive data from files, APIs, messages, or governed remote sources. |
| Normalize | Validate, transform, enrich, and map data into canonical schemas. |
| Govern | Apply tenant isolation, permissions, audit, versioning, search, and workflow. |
| Deliver | Export data to target systems in the format and contract they require. |
DaaS is powerful because one canonical data model can serve many systems without every system writing its own import, validation, transformation, search, and export logic.

sections.heading: What DaaS Means In Nodics
paragraphs: DaaS combines multiple Nodics capabilities:
The value is not one API endpoint. The value is a governed data platform that keeps source data, normalized data, business-ready data, and exported data under clear ownership.
items: tenants for company or customer separation;
validators and interceptors for data quality;
services and facades for business behavior;
runtime governance for controlled activation, audit, and rollback;
provider modules for databases, messaging, cache, search, files, and external systems.

sections.heading: Business Use Case: Product Catalog Information Center
paragraphs: A strong DaaS use case is a Product Catalog Information Center.
In this model, Nodics manages product catalog data for multiple companies, multiple business lines, and multiple consuming systems.
Example:
The same canonical product data can serve many applications without forcing every application to own its own copy of the import, validation, enrichment, and export logic.
items: Each tenant may manage catalogs for electronics, apparel, groceries, spare parts, or other product domains.
Product data may arrive from ERP, supplier files, PIM systems, spreadsheets, APIs, events, or manual imports.
Nodics validates, normalizes, enriches, classifies, indexes, and governs that data.
Target systems receive exports shaped to their own contract, such as ecommerce storefronts, marketplaces, ERP systems, analytics platforms, or partner feeds.

sections.heading: Where To Build A DaaS Feature
paragraphs:
| Need | Write/configure here |
| --- | --- |
| Canonical data shape | Owning module `src/schemas/schemas.js` |
| Source file or payload mapping | Import headers/data definitions and import services |
| Validation/transformation | Import processors, validators, interceptors, pipelines, services |
| Tenant/company isolation | Tenant configuration, schemas, services, cache/search/import/export tests |
| Product/catalog grouping | Catalog/content modules and project catalog schemas |
| Search/retrieval | `src/search/indexes.js` and search provider configuration |
| Scheduled pickup | CronJob plus import service |
| Target delivery | Export service/pipeline/provider module |
| Audit and run history | Import/export history services and diagnostics |
| Customer-specific mapping | Project module override, not framework source |

sections.heading: Data Feeding Patterns
paragraphs: DaaS implementations usually receive data in two ways.

sections.heading: External Systems Push Data To Nodics
paragraphs: In this pattern, the external system calls Nodics import services and pushes data into the platform.
Use this when the source system should decide when the data is ready.
Examples:

The data still enters the Nodics import pipeline. Filters, validators, processors, interceptors, tenant resolution, access policy, events, search indexing, diagnostics, and import history remain owned by Nodics.
items: ERP pushes product, price, or inventory updates;
marketplace application pushes order or product status;
business application pushes customer or account data;
admin tool uploads an approved import payload.

sections.heading: Nodics Pulls Or Picks Up Files
paragraphs: In this pattern, the source system places files in a governed location and Nodics imports them through a scheduled process.
Use this when the source system produces batch files, cannot call Nodics APIs, or needs a periodic exchange.
Examples:
The same import pipeline processes the files after Nodics picks them up. This keeps validation, transformation, audit, tenant isolation, and downstream events consistent with push-based imports.

When direct remote pull from external locations is required, remote import adapters can stage files from SFTP, object storage, partner API, HTTPS pull, or enterprise file gateway before the normal import pipeline runs. That adapter remains a governed project or provider responsibility and must not become a generic open framework endpoint.
items: supplier CSV files are placed in a configured import folder;
ERP exports Excel files every night;
product catalog JSON files are placed in a governed Nodics import location;
JavaScript data definition files are placed in module-owned data folders;
a CronJob periodically triggers the import service for pending files.

sections.heading: Production Remote Import Adapter Gate
paragraphs: Remote import is a governed extension path for direct-pull data intake. It is not an open endpoint where a caller can provide arbitrary URLs, credentials, or executable definitions.

The framework keeps remote import disabled by default. A project, provider, environment, server, or tenant layer must explicitly register the source and transport configuration before remote import can run.
A production remote import adapter must:

Supported adapter examples can include SFTP, object storage, partner APIs, HTTPS pull, message-backed file drops, or enterprise file gateways. The adapter choice belongs to the project or provider layer because each production source has different authentication, contract, retry, latency, and audit expectations.

Remote input may provide source data. It must not provide schema definitions, router definitions, service code, executable configuration, or generated artifacts. Headers and processing rules must still come from trusted active Nodics modules.
items: be owned by a clear project or provider module;
implement the standard adapter service contract;
stage only data files in the server-owned staging location;
return file descriptors with SHA-256 checksums;
keep endpoints, credentials, tokens, and secret paths in governed configuration or secret storage;
enforce tenant, module, and source allowlists;
respect timeout, retry, file-count, file-size, total-size, extension, checksum, and cleanup policies;
produce sanitized diagnostics and import run history;
prove deterministic behavior through contract tests;
prove live behavior through guarded integration or release tests before any public route is exposed.

sections.heading: Canonical Data Model
paragraphs: DaaS needs a canonical model that represents the business truth inside Nodics.
For product catalog data, the canonical model may include:
Schemas define this model. Generated APIs, services, validators, search indexes, import/export behavior, and tests come from those source definitions.

If one company, tenant, catalog, or application needs additional fields, use layered schema extension through the owning project or tenant layer. Do not hardcode one customer's product model into a reusable framework module.

sections.heading: Tenant And Catalog Separation
paragraphs: Tenants separate company or customer boundaries.
Catalogs separate business domains, product domains, or application-facing data areas inside those boundaries.
For example:
Tenant context protects data ownership. Catalog structure organizes business meaning. Both must be visible in schemas, import definitions, export definitions, search indexes, permissions, and tests.
items: Company A can own an electronics catalog and an apparel catalog.
Company B can own a spare-parts catalog.
A marketplace application can consume a subset of approved products.
A storefront can consume another subset with storefront-specific attributes.
An analytics system can receive an enriched export with additional classification fields.

sections.heading: Data Validation And Enrichment
paragraphs: Imported data usually needs more than field mapping.
Nodics can validate and enrich data through:
Examples:
Validation and enrichment logic belongs in owned services, processors, validators, interceptors, or pipelines. Do not hide transformation rules in one-off scripts or generated output.
items: Normalize supplier color names into a controlled color catalog.
Map source categories into the tenant's catalog hierarchy.
Mark records for manual review when confidence is low.
Emit events after successful import or approval.

sections.heading: Pipeline, Interceptor, And Event Flow
paragraphs: DaaS is process-oriented.
A product import may flow like this:
Pipelines define ordered process behavior. Interceptors protect lifecycle points. Events allow other modules to react without forcing every step into one service method.
items: Receive source file or source payload.
Emit events for indexing, approval, workflow, or export readiness.
Record import diagnostics and run history.

sections.heading: Search And Retrieval
paragraphs: DaaS data must be easy to retrieve.
Nodics search indexes can support:
Search index definitions belong to the module that owns the searchable data. Search provider details belong behind provider modules and layered configuration.

sections.heading: Export Contracts
paragraphs: DaaS becomes valuable when it can serve many target systems.
Each export flow defines:
For example, the same canonical product record may be exported differently:

Export processors are responsible for matching target contracts. Do not change the canonical model just to satisfy one target system. Add or override export processors, field mappings, configuration, or project-layer services for the target.
items: ecommerce storefront export with display attributes and media;
ERP export with inventory and financial identifiers;
marketplace export with channel-specific category mapping;
analytics export with enriched classification attributes;
partner feed export with only approved public fields.

sections.heading: Runtime Governance
paragraphs: DaaS changes often affect many records and many consuming systems.
Use runtime governance when a change needs:
Runtime governance is useful for catalog activation, publish flows, runtime configuration, export rule changes, source mapping changes, and data quality policy changes.

sections.heading: Security And Audit
paragraphs: DaaS must protect data boundaries.
Important controls include:
Never put credentials, tenant secrets, endpoint secrets, or target-system tokens in source-controlled files.
items: integration release gates for live providers.

paragraphs: When designing a DaaS flow, define:

sections.heading: What To Avoid
paragraphs: Avoid:
items: creating a `daas` module just because the business pattern is called DaaS;
forcing DaaS behavior into one generic service;
hardcoding one source-system contract into framework import logic;
hardcoding one target-system contract into the canonical model;
making external provider behavior required for basic tests;
treating the Postman DaaS reference as a missing framework module.
